cim: Plato Was Right: Artificial Intelligence Makes the Philosopher-King More Urgent
cim_eredeti: Plato Was Right: Artificial Intelligence Makes the Philosopher-King More Urgent
szoveg_eredeti:
Plato has been unfashionable for approximately two thousand years, which is usually a sign that a philosopher has said something important. His most notorious political proposition — that there will be no end to the troubles of states until philosophers become kings, or kings genuinely become philosophers — has generally been treated by modern liberal societies as an embarrassing relic of aristocratic Athens. We prefer elections, opinion polls, focus groups, television debates, political consultants and politicians whose principal intellectual accomplishment is remembering which camera to look into. The philosopher-king seems sinister, elitist and faintly ridiculous. Yet artificial intelligence may rehabilitate him.

The reason is not that philosophers are particularly pleasant people. They frequently are not. Nor is it that philosophy departments ought to be placed in charge of nuclear weapons, central banks and intelligence agencies, an experiment that might rapidly vindicate every objection ever made to Plato. The reason is more disturbing. Humanity is constructing instruments of almost inconceivable intellectual power while the intellectual quality of many of the people governing advanced societies appears, to put the matter politely, stubbornly human. The mismatch between the sophistication of our instruments and the wisdom of those operating them is becoming dangerous.

Artificial intelligence does not merely increase the amount of information available to political leaders. It increases their capacity to act upon information, to manipulate populations, to anticipate behaviour, to organise bureaucracies, to conduct warfare, to supervise economies and eventually perhaps to make decisions at speeds that human institutions cannot meaningfully follow. We are therefore approaching an historical situation in which mediocre people may wield extraordinary intelligence. Plato would have recognised the problem immediately.

Plato did not believe that clever people should rule merely because they were clever. Athens was full of clever people. Sophists could make persuasive arguments for almost anything, politicians could excite crowds, merchants could calculate profits and generals could devise ingenious campaigns. Cleverness was plentiful; wisdom was not. The distinction lies at the centre of The Republic.

The philosopher is not simply somebody possessing information. He is somebody trained to ask what knowledge is for. He distinguishes appearance from reality, appetite from value and immediate advantage from the good. Most importantly, Plato’s ideal ruler does not desperately want to rule. The desire for political power is itself evidence that somebody may be psychologically unsuitable to possess it.

One suspects Plato would have found the modern election campaign baffling. Candidates now spend enormous quantities of money attempting to prove that they want power more intensely than their competitors. They shake thousands of hands, repeat slogans selected through polling, hire professionals to manipulate their appearances and spend months explaining why the catastrophe facing civilisation can be prevented only by placing them personally in charge of it. For Plato, this would have been an excellent method of identifying precisely the people who should not govern.

Modern constitutional democracy has nevertheless possessed an extraordinarily powerful answer to Plato. We do not need rulers to be exceptionally wise because we can constrain them. Elections remove them, courts frustrate them, legislatures argue with them, journalists expose them and bureaucracies slow them down. Constitutions tell them that there are certain things they may not do even when they are convinced those things would be splendid ideas. The liberal state is therefore built upon a less romantic conception of humanity than Plato’s republic: instead of asking how we might find a perfectly wise ruler, it asks how we might survive an imperfect one.

That has worked surprisingly well. Artificial intelligence complicates the arrangement because it may make imperfect rulers vastly more powerful. The constitutional machinery designed to restrain ordinary human folly may prove inadequate when ordinary human folly is equipped with extraordinary computational capacity.

The traditional fool in government was limited by friction. He might have wanted to reorganise the economy overnight, arrest thousands of supposed enemies, manipulate the information received by every citizen or calculate the precise vulnerabilities of millions of individuals, but the administrative machinery required to accomplish these things was slow and expensive. Human bureaucracies had to collect information, process documents, issue instructions and enforce decisions. Incompetence itself sometimes functioned as an accidental constitutional safeguard.

Artificial intelligence removes much of that friction. A government equipped with sufficiently advanced AI could potentially analyse immense populations in real time. It could correlate financial records, movements, communications, facial recognition, political preferences and social relationships. It could generate personalised propaganda for individual citizens rather than broadcasting the same message to everyone. It could identify emerging political opposition before that opposition had organised itself, while optimising taxation, military mobilisation, policing and economic intervention on scales previously unimaginable.

None of these possibilities requires the machine itself to become tyrannical. Human beings are perfectly capable of supplying the tyranny. The fashionable nightmare is that artificial intelligence becomes malevolent and decides to dominate humanity, but the historically more familiar nightmare is that a human being decides to dominate other human beings and discovers that artificial intelligence is extremely useful. A malicious superintelligence would undoubtedly be alarming; a stupid politician with access to a superintelligence may be the more immediate danger.

For most of human history, sophisticated intellectual production was expensive. Writing a competent legal memorandum required lawyers. Designing a bridge required engineers. Producing propaganda required writers, artists and printers. Analysing military intelligence required large staffs. Governments therefore accumulated bureaucracies containing specialised human knowledge because intelligence was scarce, slow and costly to reproduce.

Artificial intelligence is making many forms of intellectual production dramatically cheaper. It can already produce plausible legal analysis, computer code, economic summaries, strategic plans, speeches, translations and administrative documents within seconds, and these capacities will improve. Something peculiar follows from this development: intelligence, or at least many outward manifestations of intelligence, may become abundant, while wisdom will not.

This distinction may define politics in the artificial intelligence age. The world may soon possess more analysis than anybody can read, more predictions than anybody can evaluate and more arguments than anybody can answer. Every minister will be surrounded by machines capable of producing extraordinarily sophisticated justifications for almost any proposed course of action. The problem will no longer be finding somebody capable of constructing an argument; it will be finding somebody capable of recognising when an impressive argument is nonsense. That is, in substantial part, a philosophical skill.

There is another reason Plato suddenly seems unnervingly contemporary. His most famous metaphor describes prisoners chained inside a cave watching shadows projected upon a wall. Having never seen anything else, they mistake the shadows for reality. Modern civilisation has spent the past thirty years constructing the most sophisticated cave in history.

We increasingly encounter the world through screens.
